newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Bougainville peace talks face uncertain future.
newsitem.headline: Bougainville peace talks face uncertain future.

text.p: Peace talks in New Zealand aimed at ending nine years of secessionist violence on Papua New Guinea's Bougainville Island will need to overcome the absence of key figures in the conflict and the poor track record of previous attempts.

Representatives of the three main groups in the Bougainville war, the PNG-backed Bougainville Transitional Government (BTG), the Bougainville Interim Government (BIG) and its associate the Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRN), will begin formal discussions on Monday at Burnham Military Camp near the South Island city of Christchurch.

It is understood the talks will discuss the creation of a neutral zone on the Papua New Guinean island, policing by a Pacific peacekeeping force and where substantive peace negotiations can take place.
But the success of the meeting is uncertain after shadowy BIG leader Francis Ona failed to show up and revelations that there will be no top-level PNG government representation.
Ona has refused to attend previous internationally brokered peace talks and has so far failed to honour commitments made by his representatives.
The goodwill expressed by both sides in the conflict was also tainted on the eve of the summit when 14 delegates were prevented from attending after a helicopter sent to pick them up was fired at.

New Zealand Foreign Affairs Minister Don McKinnon stressed the preliminary nature of the talks, which he said were designed to broker dialogue between Bougainville representatives on neutral territory.
"I'm fully aware there are some who would wish to be here but are unable to come," McKinnon told the 50 delegates on their arrival in Christchurch on Saturday.
"But nevertheless ... I hope that in the days ahead you will find some common ground."

Thousands have died in the bloody Bougainville conflict since landowners revolted in 1989 over environmental damage caused by the huge Panguna copper mine and the royalties received from it. The mine is owned by a unit of Anglo-Australian giant RTZ Corp.
BIG/BRA delegation leader Joseph Kabui said attempts since the early 1990s to find a solution to the Bougainville war had been marred by time and process constraints.

"We have been through many other attempts to find solutions to the great tragedy that has overtaken our people. In each one we have learned valuable lessons, but none has brought us fully to resolution," Kabui said.
"We are very optimistic that the process we hope to set in place here will continue to steer us in the direction of an eventual and an acceptable solution to the Bougainville question."
The peace talks are expected to last at least a week and it was hoped more delegates would arrive during the week.
"We do not expect a quick answer to the Bougainville crisis, which has divided our people and brought about suffering, sorrow and death," said Gerard Sinato, BTG premier.
"But we hope to strengthen our path to peace in our deliberations. We are in New Zealand to continue our search for lasting peace on Bougainville."
